bugs: failed() clears sync_started_at for every id unconditionally. If a job outlives the 15-minute claim (for example it sits in the SQS backlog) and the rows have been re-claimed, the old job's failure wipes the new claim and the rows get dispatched a second time. Probe confirmed 2 jobs pushed (app/Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:85)

Timestamps are second-precision and synced_at is set to the claim time, so an edit made in the same second as the claim while the push is running is never re-synced. Probe confirmed. The same weakness exists in all three implementations
antipatterns: The timestamp is interpolated into raw SQL: DB::raw("coalesce(sync_started_at, '{$fallback}')") (app/Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:75). A binding or a plain column reference would be cleaner
The rate-limiter test only checks that the middleware count is 1 and that the limiter exists. The config it sets is never used (tests/Feature/StockSyncTest.php:239-245)
A global const STOCK_URL in the test file collides if another test file defines the same name (tests/Feature/StockSyncTest.php:12)
Fully qualified \DateTimeInterface instead of an import (app/Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:30)
strengths: The only implementation that throttles proactively: RateLimited('storefront') middleware with a RateLimiter::for limit in AppServiceProvider, shared through Redis. A probe showed the second job is released (63s), not failed. It also reacts to 429 with a capped Retry-After (30-300s)

The claim runs in a transaction with lockForUpdate, toBase() leaves updated_at untouched, and the schedule uses onOneServer plus withoutOverlapping(5). This is the right setup for three schedulers on Redis
synced_at is set to the claim time, so edits made after the claim stay ready, and a test covers it
retryUntil of 10 minutes stays well inside the 15-minute claim window. Timeout, MaxExceptions and Backoff are set with Laravel 13 attributes, and the job uses tooManyRequests() and acceptJson()
Mark-synced and disable run in one transaction. The idiomatic $allocations->whereIn('sku',$missing)->modelKeys()
Full Pest suite (24 tests): scope cases, chunking of 250 rows into [100,100,50], idempotency, 429 asserted with withFakeQueueInteractions, 500, failed() leading to re-dispatch, schedule assertions

bugs: Nothing throttles requests before they are sent; the job only reacts to 429. At peak about 50 jobs hit an API that is slow and rate-limited all at once, and each 429 release uses up the 10-minute retryUntil budget. Rows are not lost (failed() frees them), but sustained 429s cause churn and delays

The schedule has onOneServer but no withoutOverlapping (routes/console.php). The claim is an optimistic UPDATE followed by a re-select WHERE sync_started_at = $claimedAt at second precision. Two overlapping runs in the same second would re-select each other's rows and dispatch them twice (app/Console/Commands/DispatchStockSync.php:25-29)
failed() unconditionally clears claims that may belong to a newer job. Probe confirmed a duplicate dispatch (app/Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:84)
An edit in the same second as the claim during the push is lost, because of second-precision timestamps (shared by all three)
antipatterns: Claiming without a lock relies on timestamp equality to decide who owns the rows. This is fragile compared with lockForUpdate in a transaction (app/Console/Commands/DispatchStockSync.php:21-29)
The disable and mark-synced updates are not wrapped in a transaction (app/Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:65-79)
The job uses the full get() instead of selecting only the needed columns, and the request has no acceptJson()
A global const STOCK_URL in the test file (tests/Feature/StockSyncTest.php:11)
strengths: synced_at => DB::raw('sync_started_at') is a clean way to set the sync time to the claim time. The job also re-checks whereNotNull('sync_started_at'), so stale or duplicate runs do nothing
FailOnTimeout, MaxExceptions, Backoff and Timeout are set as attributes. retryUntil stays within the claim window. The Retry-After delay is capped at 300 with a default of 60

The best test suite (27 tests): a dataset for the Retry-After cap and default, edit-during-push, idempotency asserting the HTTP request was sent once, skipping unclaimed or disabled rows, and an end-to-end run on the sync queue

bugs: The 429 release delay is uncapped: Retry-After 3600 gives release(3600) (probe confirmed), well past the 14-minute retryUntil. The job then expires and goes to failed() rather than retrying in a controlled way (app/Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:47)

retryUntil is now()+14 minutes, measured from dispatch, and Timeout is 60s. An attempt that starts near the deadline can run to the 15-minute mark, so the dispatcher may re-claim rows that are still in flight. The margin is too thin (app/Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:25)
Nothing throttles requests before they are sent; it only reacts to 429. About 50 concurrent jobs at peak will hammer a rate-limited API
failed() unconditionally clears claims that may belong to a newer job. Probe confirmed a duplicate dispatch (app/Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:66)
synced_at is the job start time, so an in-flight edit in the same second as the start is lost (a shared weakness, and the window is a little wider here than with the claim time)
antipatterns: partition() with in_array, where $allocations->whereIn('sku', $missing) would do (app/Jobs/PushStockAllocations.php:55)
The 429 test hand-mocks the Job contract with Mockery instead of using the built-in withFakeQueueInteractions()/assertReleased() (tests/Feature/StockSyncTest.php:151-153)
The two final updates are not in a transaction
The ExampleTest scaffolding is left in place, and a global const STOCK_URL sits in the test file
strengths: The dispatcher matches impl-1's: a locked transactional claim, toBase() keeps updated_at untouched, and the schedule uses onOneServer plus withoutOverlapping
Http::baseUrl from config with acceptJson and a timeout, and selected columns only
Compact code with a concise scope and factory states

v.rationale:
I rank impl-1 first, impl-2 second and impl-3 third. All three suites pass (24, 27 and 16 tests), and I deleted every probe file afterwards.

All three share the same core design: a readyToSync scope, a claim made with toBase() so updated_at is not bumped, a failed() that frees the claim, and retryUntil kept inside the 15-minute window. Probes found the same two weaknesses in every one:
- An edit in the same second as the claim (impl-1, impl-2) or the job start (impl-3) is lost, because timestamps only have second precision.
- A stale job's failed() can wipe a newer claim, which causes a duplicate dispatch.

What separates them:

**impl-1** is the only one that handles the storefront's rate limit before requests go out. It uses RateLimited middleware with a named limiter shared through Redis; a probe showed the second job is released, not failed. On top of that it caps Retry-After handling, claims rows inside a locked transaction, schedules with onOneServer plus withoutOverlapping, and leaves a 5-minute safety margin on retryUntil. Its flaws are small: raw SQL built with string interpolation, and one weak limiter test.

**impl-2** has the strongest tests and some neat touches: synced_at is copied from sync_started_at in SQL, the job re-checks that its rows are still claimed, and it uses FailOnTimeout. It only reacts to 429s rather than throttling, though. It also claims rows without a lock and has no withoutOverlapping, so two overlapping runs in the same second could dispatch the same rows twice.

**impl-3** has a dispatcher as sound as impl-1's. But it only reacts to 429s, does not cap the Retry-After delay (a probe gave release(3600), far past its own retryUntil), and leaves too thin a margin between its 14-minute retryUntil plus 60s timeout and the 15-minute claim expiry. Its tests are the thinnest: no edit-during-push case, and a hand-written Mockery mock where the built-in withFakeQueueInteractions() would do.
